meta.title: Forest Futures
meta.subtitle: A strategic foresight game for forest leaders
meta.credits: Evolved from “IMPACT: a foresight game – forestry edition” (2019) by the Strategic Foresight Group — David N. Bengston and Lynne M. Westphal (USDA Forest Service, Northern Research Station) and Michael J. Dockry and Jason S. Crabtree (University of Minnesota) — itself an adaptation of IMPACT, designed by Idea Couture in collaboration with Policy Horizons Canada.
meta.notice: Signals are drawn from real-world sources; their effects in the game are speculative and meant to provoke discussion, not to predict. This is an independent tool, not an official product of USDA or any agency.

eras.name: Now
eras.description: Trends already in motion and decisions already made. High certainty, little time.

eras.name: Near
eras.description: Emerging changes that are plausible within a planning cycle or two.

eras.name: Far
eras.description: Weak signals and wildcards. Low certainty, high consequence.

signals.title: The 10 a.m. rule, take two
signals.signal: Interior ordered the new U.S. Wildland Fire Service to fully suppress every wildfire it manages, echoing the 1935 '10 a.m. rule'; the Forest Service also operates under a full-suppression policy.

primary.text: More starts are caught small, but fewer fires burn for benefit; fuels keep building and future fires get harder to stop.

secondary.text: In the short run, fewer fires reach towns and managed-fire smoke days drop, even as fuels build.

signals.prompt: When is putting every fire out the riskiest choice, and who should decide?

source.title: As wildfires worsen, Trump administration revives discredited policy to stomp out all fires quickly

signals.title: Fuels work drops a third
signals.signal: An outside analysis found Forest Service fuel-treatment acres fell from over 4 million in 2024 to about 2.6 million in 2025, and prescribed burning roughly halved; the agency cites fire demands and hurricane debris, critics cite staff losses.

primary.text: Untreated acres pile up just as hot, dry seasons return; the odds of severe, fast-moving fire climb.

secondary.text: Remove 1 point from a domain hurt most by the treatment backlog, and explain how the harm unfolds.

signals.prompt: How do we rebuild treatment pace when the same people are pulled to fight fires?

source.title: Trump administration falls behind on wildfire prevention with risky fire season ahead

signals.title: Clearing the air for good fire
signals.signal: The Senate unanimously passed a bill easing Clean Air Act penalties on states for prescribed burns and creating grants to protect schools and community buildings from smoke; it must be reconciled with a broader House bill.

primary.text: States schedule more prescribed burns without fear of air-quality violations, and scarce burn windows actually get used.

secondary.text: Smoke-ready schools and shelters give residents cleaner air on the worst days.

signals.prompt: How do we share smoke trade-offs with communities before the burn, not after?

source.title: Wildfire bill to ease path for controlled burns passes Senate

signals.title: A backstop for the burn boss
signals.signal: Texas A&M Forest Service launched a temporary, state-run self-insurance pool for certified prescribed burn managers, after commercial coverage for them grew scarce or vanished statewide.

primary.text: Public liability pools spread across states, and private burners put good fire back on millions of acres.

secondary.text: The state now carries the claims risk, so one escaped burn could land on taxpayers and lawmakers.

signals.prompt: Who should carry the risk when good fire goes bad?

source.title: Texas A&M Forest Service Launches Prescribed Burn Manager Insurance Program

signals.title: Smoke alarms in orbit
signals.signal: The first three operational FireSat satellites reached orbit in 2026, able to spot fires about 5 meters across through smoke and cloud; backers aim for hourly global revisits by 2029.

primary.text: Near-constant detection catches starts early; initial attack wins more often and fewer fires escape.

secondary.text: Add 1 point to a domain that gains from near-real-time fire data, and explain how.

signals.prompt: If every start is seen within an hour, what changes in how we staff and decide?

source.title: Muon Space Deploys First Three Operational FireSat Satellites for Earth Fire Alliance

signals.title: Prairie fire, extra large
signals.signal: Nebraska's Morrill Fire burned about 642,000 acres in March 2026, the largest in state history; on some rural starts, NOAA's experimental AI satellite detections arrived before firefighters were dispatched.

primary.text: Megafires spread beyond the West; plains and eastern states face huge fires with thin crews and few plans.

secondary.text: Remove 1 point from a domain a plains megafire would hit hardest, and explain.

signals.prompt: Is our mutual-aid system ready for megafires where we rarely expect them?

source.title: NOAA's Wildfire Detection System a “Game Changer” for Nebraska's Record-Breaking Morrill Fire

signals.title: Smoke gets in our lungs
signals.signal: A 2025 Nature study estimates wildfire smoke already contributes to about 40,000 U.S. deaths a year and could exceed 71,000 annually by 2050 under high emissions.

primary.text: Smoke, not flame, becomes wildfire's largest toll, pressing agencies to manage fire for air quality as well as acres.

secondary.text: Mounting health costs give fire and air agencies a shared case for prescribed-fire and smoke-readiness funding.

signals.prompt: Should smoke health outcomes become a core measure of fire program success?

source.title: Wildfire smoke could soon kill 71,000 Americans every year

signals.title: Alaska's fire math doubles
signals.signal: A 2026 study projects area burned in Alaska rising under every emissions scenario, more than doubling under high emissions, with up to eightfold increases in parts of Alaska's Arctic and west.

primary.text: Northern megafires lengthen the national season and pull crews and aircraft north when the West needs them.

secondary.text: Burning boreal forest and peat release vast stores of carbon, accelerating warming.

signals.prompt: How do we share scarce crews when the fire season never ends somewhere?

source.title: Study Outlines a Range of Possible Fire Futures for Alaska

signals.title: Fires that never grow up
signals.signal: In XPRIZE Wildfire finals in Alaska, teams had to autonomously find and extinguish fires within 10 minutes of ignition across about 1,000 square kilometers; award winner Dryad plans pilots in 2027.

primary.text: Sensor-and-drone networks snuff most starts within minutes; escaped fires become rare near communities and critical watersheds.

secondary.text: Move 1 point between domains to show who gains and who loses when robots fight fire. Explain.

signals.prompt: If machines catch every start, how do we keep beneficial fire on the land?

source.title: Dryad Networks Wins XPRIZE Wildfire Award for Drones, Sensor Networks

signals.title: One rulebook, fewer comment periods
signals.signal: USDA's department-wide NEPA procedures took effect in April 2026, centralizing categorical exclusions and leaving public comment on most environmental assessments and exclusions to the responsible official's discretion.

primary.text: Projects clear review faster and small teams move more work, though thinner records raise litigation risk.

secondary.text: Some publics feel shut out of decisions; trust erodes where comment was once routine.

signals.prompt: How do we keep people engaged when the law no longer requires it?

source.title: US Department of Agriculture Finalizes Updated NEPA Procedures

signals.title: Appropriators hold the line, for now
signals.signal: The FY2027 request would cut the Forest Service line about 75%, largely by moving firefighting to Interior; House appropriators kept fire in the agency and raised its total about 2%. A stopgap runs through December 11.

primary.text: Bipartisan appropriators keep core programs funded, buying time, though stopgaps and shutdown threats still freeze planning.

secondary.text: Protect one domain: name the line item appropriators shield this era and why it survives.

signals.prompt: What would we cut first if a shutdown hit during fire season?

source.title: Interior, Environment, and Related Agencies: Overview of FY2027 Appropriations (R49292)

signals.title: Fire borrowing's comeback tour
signals.signal: The 2018 wildfire funding fix, a disaster cap adjustment worth about $2.9 billion for the Forest Service and Interior in FY2026, expires after 2027, and Congress has not agreed how to extend it, reviving the risk of raiding non-fire accounts.

primary.text: Without an extension, big fire years again drain restoration, recreation and research budgets mid-season.

secondary.text: Remove 1 point from the domain whose budget gets borrowed first, and explain the trade.

signals.prompt: Which partner commitments would we break if fire borrowing returned next summer?

source.title: Forest Service nears a return to 'fire borrowing' unless Congress acts

signals.title: The roadless rule hits the road
signals.signal: USDA proposed rescinding the 2001 Roadless Rule across 44.7 million acres, about 30 percent of national forest land, keeping Idaho and Colorado's state rules; comments closed in October and lawsuits are expected once final.

primary.text: Years of litigation and shifting rules cloud planning in roadless areas, whichever way the courts rule.

secondary.text: Move 1 point between domains, say recreation to wood or the reverse, and explain who gains access and who loses.

signals.prompt: Where would new roads reduce fire risk, and where would they add to it?

source.title: Trump Administration Proposes to Rescind Roadless Rule
source.publisher: Harvard Law School Environmental & Energy Law Program

signals.title: One flag for wildland fire
signals.signal: Interior launched the U.S. Wildland Fire Service in January 2026, merging its bureaus' fire programs; Congress declined to fund folding in Forest Service firefighters and ordered a feasibility study first.

primary.text: A single federal fire agency, authorized with clear ties to land managers, simplifies command, budgets and accountability.

secondary.text: Years of transition churn, from new chains of command to new duty stations, push some veterans out.

signals.prompt: What must stay connected between fire and land management if fire gets its own agency?

source.title: Trump administration stands up consolidated federal firefighting agency over bipartisan congressional reservations

signals.title: Fix Our Forests, still parked
signals.signal: The Fix Our Forests Act passed the House 279-141 in January 2025 and cleared Senate Agriculture 18-5, but still awaits a floor vote; backers want it attached to the defense authorization bill.

primary.text: A version becomes law: faster reviews, a federal wildfire intelligence center and a new community wildfire risk-reduction program.

secondary.text: Add 1 point to a domain that gains when fireshed projects move faster, and explain how.

signals.prompt: Which stalled projects would move first, and are we staffed to deliver them?

source.title: Wildfire bill stalls in Senate as insurance market keeps shrinking

signals.title: Utilities seek a fire shield
signals.signal: About half of Western states have enacted some limit on utility wildfire liability, usually tied to approved mitigation plans; insurers warn the costs shift to homeowners, and some fire survivors oppose the limits.

primary.text: Clear liability rules keep utilities solvent and paying for line hardening, vegetation clearing and smarter shutoffs.

secondary.text: Survivors recover less after utility-caused fires, and homeowner premiums rise to absorb the gap.

signals.prompt: What should a utility owe if it followed its plan and still started a fire?

source.title: Electric companies are fighting across the West to limit their blame for wildfires
source.publisher: KJZZ / Mountain West News Bureau (via KUNC)

signals.title: 'For sale' signs on public land
signals.signal: A 2025 Senate budget-bill draft would have required selling 600,000 to 1.2 million acres of BLM land within a decade, partly for housing; it was withdrawn amid public backlash and Senate rules problems.

primary.text: Disposal returns in a future budget fight; scattered sales fragment management and access across the West.

secondary.text: Sold parcels could open land for housing near crowded towns, the benefit sale backers point to.

signals.prompt: Which parcels near our communities are most at risk, and who would defend them?

source.title: Federal land sale withdrawn from Senate's version of the Big Beautiful Bill
source.publisher: Wyoming Public Radio / Mountain West News Bureau (via KUNC)

signals.title: States take the wheel
signals.signal: The Forest Service held 540 Good Neighbor agreements in FY2025, 426 of them with 39 states plus others with counties and Tribes, and partners may keep timber revenue for restoration through FY2028.

primary.text: Cross-boundary agreements mature into shared management, with states and Tribes running much of the work on federal land.

secondary.text: State, county and Tribal staff stretch thin running work on land they do not own.

signals.prompt: What capacity would our state need to run federal projects at scale?

source.title: The Good Neighbor Authority on Federal Lands: In Brief (R49480)

signals.title: States first, FEMA second
signals.signal: A Trump-appointed FEMA Review Council recommended raising the damage threshold for federal disaster aid by more than half and paying states lump sums, giving states more control and more of the burden.

primary.text: Federal aid covers only the biggest disasters; states and counties absorb mid-sized fires, floods and recovery costs.

secondary.text: Protect one domain: name what your state would fund first when federal disaster aid shrinks.

signals.prompt: If federal disaster aid shrank tomorrow, what would our state stop doing?

source.title: A Trump council recommends overhauling FEMA. Here are 3 key changes

signals.title: Bigger targets, thinner ranks
signals.signal: GAO found the Forest Service workforce fell about 20 percent in 2025, with some forests missing 40 percent or more of timber staff, just as an executive order raised harvest targets.

primary.text: Sale preparation, contracting and planning skills thin out; remaining staff juggle several jobs and burn out.

secondary.text: Timber sales lag targets, leaving mills short of federal logs.

signals.prompt: Which skills would take us longest to rebuild if they walked out the door?

source.title: Forest Service: Opportunities Exist to Improve Timber Sale Management (GAO-26-107993)

signals.title: The raise that refilled the crews
signals.signal: The Forest Service reported about 11,550 seasonal fire staff trained or ready in June 2026, roughly 200 above its goal, crediting recent firefighter pay raises, even as it lost nearly 6,000 permanent staff.

primary.text: Competitive pay keeps seasonal crews full and steadies recruitment, even as support ranks thin.

secondary.text: Permanent raises add a recurring cost that squeezes other programs when budgets stay flat.

signals.prompt: Pay fixed recruitment; what would fix retention of mid-career leaders?

source.title: As western fires erupt, Trump's Forest Service says it's now fully staffed

signals.title: Pack the lab, or quit
signals.signal: USDA's plan to move Forest Service headquarters to Salt Lake City, replace regional offices with state offices and close about two dozen research stations was halted by a federal judge in October 2026; the ruling is under appeal.

primary.text: Scientists and specialists unwilling to relocate leave; decades of local expertise and field relationships walk out.

secondary.text: USDA projects lower overhead; if the savings hold, some dollars could shift toward field work.

signals.prompt: How would our partnerships change if the nearest federal scientists moved 1,000 miles away?

source.title: Agriculture secretary says agency is “full-bore ahead” on Forest Service reorganization

signals.title: Thin bench on the fireline
signals.signal: Federal officials warned of a 15 percent drop in available hotshot crews in 2026, and only 38 teams could handle the largest, fastest fires, down from 44 two years earlier.

primary.text: Leadership gaps compound; too few crew bosses and incident commanders for longer, overlapping fire seasons.

secondary.text: Remove 1 point from a domain that suffers when experienced fire leaders are scarce, and explain.

signals.prompt: Who are our next incident commanders, and what are we doing to keep them?

source.title: Federal Job Cuts Are Making Wildfires Harder to Fight
source.publisher: The New York Times (via GV Wire)

signals.title: Forestry's new farm team
signals.signal: A Western forestry association launched a four-state initiative linking students, schools and employers, with about $450,000 in early industry pledges, citing a trend of two trades entrants for every five retirees.

primary.text: Regional career pathways steady the supply of loggers, foresters and technicians for public and private lands.

secondary.text: Contractors and mills find trained operators, keeping harvest and restoration capacity alive.

signals.prompt: What would make our agency a young person's first-choice employer?

source.title: Regional Forestry Workforce Initiative Gains Momentum Across the Northwest

signals.title: Drone pilots join the engine
signals.signal: Aspen's fire district won an FAA waiver in October 2026 to fly AI-assisted firefighting drones once training ends, aiming to be the first department to operate them independently; they remain untested on real wildfires.

primary.text: Crews add drone pilots and data roles, extending reach at night and over terrain too risky for people.

secondary.text: Add 1 point to a domain that benefits when crews can fly drones, and explain how.

signals.prompt: Which skills should our next hires bring that our current crews lack?

source.title: Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones

signals.title: Firefighting, by contract
signals.signal: USDA's 2026 wildfire readiness memo counted more than 22,000 contracted resources from about 2,500 vendors alongside 28,000-plus mobilizable responders, underscoring reliance on private engines, crews and aircraft.

primary.text: Contractors supply surge capacity on demand, filling gaps left by a smaller federal workforce.

secondary.text: Contract costs climb, and thin agency staff struggle to oversee quality, safety and accountability.

signals.prompt: What should never be contracted out, and why?

source.title: USDA increases wildfire firefighting capacity for the 2026 fire season

signals.title: Robots join the thinning crew
signals.signal: European researchers field-tested a supervised autonomous harvester that navigates forests and grasps trees for selective thinning, with a human approving each cut; it still needed human help about 9 percent of the time.

primary.text: Supervised machines take over the most dangerous cutting work, with fewer injuries and more thinning per operator.

secondary.text: Add 1 point to a domain that gains when thinning gets cheaper and safer, and explain how.

signals.prompt: If one operator runs three machines, what new jobs do we need to create?

source.title: SAHA: Supervised Autonomous HArvester for selective forest thinning
source.publisher: arXiv (ETH Zurich, University of Bonn, Prefor)

signals.title: The planner's new co-pilot
signals.signal: Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and OpenAI built a benchmark testing whether AI agents can draft cited environmental impact statement sections, drawn from 19 agencies' reviews; researchers stress human oversight remains essential.

primary.text: AI handles first drafts and record searches; specialists spend their time on judgment, field checks and people.

secondary.text: Move 1 point between domains to show who wins and who loses when AI speeds decisions. Explain.

signals.prompt: Which decisions must always carry a human name?

source.title: PermitAI public-private partnership speeds environmental review drafting tasks

signals.title: Stripes are not a good look
signals.signal: Beech leaf disease, tied to an invasive nematode, now reaches 15 states and Ontario. Fluopyram and trunk injections can save individual trees, but no forest-scale treatment exists yet.

primary.text: Beech-dominated stands thin and saplings die, an ash-borer-scale loss met only with tree-by-tree tools.

secondary.text: Remove 1 from a domain hurt as beech canopies thin. Explain the link: wildlife, recreation, streams or timber.

signals.prompt: Which beech stands are worth treating, and who pays?

source.title: Disease threatens beech trees in all Chesapeake Bay states

signals.title: Drought sets the beetle buffet
signals.signal: New Mexico's 2025 aerial survey found tree deaths tripled statewide and beetle-killed conifer acres rose 211%, mostly on national forests, as drought, heat and warm winters stressed overly dense stands.

primary.text: Drought-weakened, overstocked stands fall to bark beetles faster than crews can thin or replant.

secondary.text: Salvage and biomass buyers get a pulse of dead timber where mills are close enough.

signals.prompt: Where should thinning go first: beetle-threatened stands or fire-prone ones?

source.title: Tree deaths tripled across New Mexico in 2025 amid drought, heat
source.publisher: Grant County Beat (NM Forestry Division release)

signals.title: Chestnuts roasting on a permit
signals.signal: In August 2026 USDA APHIS deregulated Darling 54, SUNY-ESF's American chestnut engineered for blight tolerance, finding it unlikely to pose more plant pest risk than unmodified chestnut, and published responses to public comments.

primary.text: A blight-tolerant chestnut can be propagated and planted more widely, testing biotech as a restoration tool.

secondary.text: Add 1 to a domain that gains if the chestnut returns. Explain how: wildlife, mast, wood, Tribal foods or trust.

signals.prompt: What evidence and consent would you need before planting biotech trees on your lands?

source.title: USDA Deregulates American Chestnut Engineered for Enhanced Blight Tolerance

signals.title: Boot camp for baby pines
signals.signal: New Mexico broke ground in April 2026 on a Mora County reforestation center aiming for 5 million seedlings a year, grown from drought- and fire-surviving trees and hardened with drought and heat.

primary.text: Regional nurseries supply hardier seedlings at scale, improving burn-scar survival that now averages about 25%.

secondary.text: Hardened, climate-matched seedlings cost more, so planting budgets cover fewer acres each year.

signals.prompt: Should every region own its seedling pipeline, or share a few big ones?

source.title: A 'Reforestation Pipeline' in New Mexico Trains Seedlings to Survive in Burn Scars

signals.title: Pest DNA caught on the breeze
signals.signal: Ohio's Holden Forests & Gardens is testing simple traps that catch airborne eDNA from forest pests; an early sample flagged the beech leaf disease nematode, narrowing where crews should search.

primary.text: Networked eDNA sampling spots invaders early, while eradication or slow-the-spread is still possible.

secondary.text: Protect a domain that early detection shields from surprise losses. Explain what you are guarding.

signals.prompt: Who would maintain thousands of eDNA traps, and act on what they find?

source.title: What's that thing on the Emergent Tower? Holden tests new forest pest monitoring tool

signals.title: Cones short, backlog long
signals.signal: California has replanted about 16% of forest lost to high-severity fire in 2020-24. Hitting its 2030 goal needs roughly 35% more planting each year, while seed and nursery capacity lag far behind.

primary.text: Burned conifer land sits unplanted for years as cones, nursery space and planting crews run short.

secondary.text: Unplanted burn scars stop storing carbon and risk converting to shrubland.

signals.prompt: What would it take to triple seed collection in your state?

source.title: California can't replant its forests fast enough to keep up with wildfires

signals.title: Southern beetle, Yankee pines
signals.signal: Warming winters let southern pine beetle spread from New Jersey and Long Island into Massachusetts, where it killed trees on Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket; over 100,000 acres there remain at risk.

primary.text: Southern-style beetle outbreaks reach northern pine forests with little experience managing them.

secondary.text: Move 1 between domains to show who bears outbreak costs and who gains from thinning and burning. Explain.

signals.prompt: Which southern pest playbooks should northern agencies borrow now?

source.title: A tiny beetle, a big wake-up call for Massachusetts forests

signals.title: From pine forest to poison oak
signals.signal: Scientists report severe fires turning Western ponderosa forests into shrubland where seedlings no longer return; studies estimate up to 40% of Western conifer forests could become shrubland by 2100.

primary.text: Large burned areas lose conifer cover for good, shrinking habitat and seed sources across the West.

secondary.text: With fewer trees drawing water, burned basins can yield more runoff for a time, though it arrives earlier.

signals.prompt: Where would you accept a new ecosystem instead of replanting the old one?

source.title: Bigger, hotter fires are slowly erasing America's great forests
source.publisher: The Boston Globe (from The New York Times)

signals.title: Trees with relocation packages
signals.signal: Sweden's ANAFOR project is testing eight broadleaf species at 10 sites from south to north to study assisted migration, including whether trees that look healthy early fail in later droughts or frosts.

primary.text: Climate-matched seed moves north and upslope, so planted forests fit the climate they will grow into.

secondary.text: Add 1 to a domain that benefits when planted forests survive the climate ahead. Explain.

signals.prompt: Who decides which non-local trees are welcome on public lands?

source.title: Can assisted migration help Swedish forests?

signals.title: The winter that forgot to snow
signals.signal: On April 1, 2026, 65% of 1,575 western snow measurements set or tied record lows after a warm, late-starting winter, NRCS reported, with streamflow forecast near or below historical minimums.

primary.text: Reservoirs, rivers and irrigators face shortages as melt comes early and small.

secondary.text: Short ski and river seasons squeeze mountain towns and outdoor businesses.

signals.prompt: If this winter repeats, which water commitments break first?

source.title: Record Low April 1 Snowpack across Western U.S. Means Impending Water Shortages

signals.title: No deal on the Colorado
signals.signal: With basin states unable to agree, Reclamation's July 2026 final plan sets a 2027-2036 Colorado River framework with two-year rules. Lower Basin cuts total 1.25 million acre-feet yearly for 2027-28.

primary.text: Deeper cuts and year-to-year uncertainty strain cities, farms and Tribes that depend on the river.

secondary.text: Move 1 between domains to show who gains and who loses as water is reallocated. Explain.

signals.prompt: How can headwater forest management earn a seat at basin negotiations?

source.title: New federal framework charts the Colorado River's next decade

signals.title: Dams out, salmon in
signals.signal: Two years after four Klamath River dams came out, researchers count over 20,000 chinook migrating upriver into nearly 90% of their former range, though 2026 drought, heat and disease hit juveniles.

primary.text: Reconnected rivers rebuild fish runs and aquatic habitat faster than many expected.

secondary.text: Removing the dams also ended a source of carbon-free hydropower for the region.

signals.prompt: Which aging dams in your watersheds cost more than they deliver?

source.title: 20,000 Salmon Return to the Klamath—but Challenging Conditions for Recovery Remain

signals.title: Utilities buy fire insurance upstream
signals.signal: Denver Water and partners have committed $96 million to headwater forest restoration since 2010, after the utility spent over $27 million recovering from the Buffalo Creek and Hayman fires.

primary.text: Watershed thinning and burning lower the odds that post-fire sediment chokes reservoirs.

secondary.text: Add 1 to the domain that gains most when water utilities co-fund forest work. Explain who benefits.

signals.prompt: Which water utility in your state should be your next forest partner?

source.title: How Colorado's biggest water utility is approaching wildfire and its drinking water impacts

signals.title: Leave it to beavers
signals.signal: A UC Berkeley-led study estimates restored Sierra Nevada beavers could store about 120 million cubic meters of water and create roughly 2,200 square kilometers of potential wildfire refuge.

primary.text: Beaver complexes slow runoff, raise water tables and keep meadows green through drought.

secondary.text: Wet, connected beaver habitat forms green refuges that resist burning in severe fires.

signals.prompt: What would it take to welcome beavers back on your landscapes?

source.title: Beavers, an ecosystem engineer, can benefit California's Sierra Nevada
source.publisher: UC Berkeley Rausser College of Natural Resources

signals.title: Thin the trees, fill the creeks
signals.signal: Forest Service-funded modeling of four central Sierra basins found thinning could raise water yields 8-14% in drought years without much added flood risk, though understory regrowth absorbs some gains.

primary.text: Targeted thinning in dense, wet watersheds delivers measurable extra water when it is scarcest.

secondary.text: Move 1 between domains to show how thinning trades value among water, wood, fire and habitat. Explain.

signals.prompt: Could downstream water users help pay for thinning upstream?

source.title: University researchers predict improved water yields after forest thinning

signals.title: Thirsty servers in dry country
signals.signal: A University of Illinois-led study finds data-center water use is rarely disclosed, even as facilities spread across Nevada, Arizona and the Mountain West; US data centers used an estimated 17 billion gallons in 2023.

primary.text: Fast-growing, opaque industrial demand competes with towns, farms and streams for scarce supplies.

secondary.text: Remove 1 from a domain squeezed when data centers compete for water and power. Explain.

signals.prompt: Should water-hungry developments help fund the watersheds they draw on?

source.title: Data centers' water use is hard to track, raising concerns in the drought-prone West, study finds

signals.title: Snow becomes a sometimes thing
signals.signal: Western April 1 snowpack fell about 18% from 1955 to 2023. Climate Central cites projections of another 25% decline by 2050 and more frequent back-to-back snow drought years.

primary.text: Rain-dominated winters and early melt force water systems to store, recharge and ration differently.

secondary.text: Longer dry seasons stress trees and invite beetles and drought mortality.

signals.prompt: What would your forest plans look like if designed for half the snow?

source.title: Record Snow Drought Limits Western Water Supplies

signals.title: Charged clouds, unproven payoff
signals.signal: Colorado and Utah permitted a company's ground-based systems that release charged aerosols to coax precipitation. Company-cited trials claim 15-18% more rain; the first US results are still to be evaluated.

primary.text: If proven, cheap weather modification adds modest precipitation over headwater forests and reservoirs.

secondary.text: Protect one domain from this era's signals while the evidence comes in. Explain why it needs a buffer.

signals.prompt: How much evidence do you need before counting engineered rain in plans?

source.title: Ionization weather modification tech expands in Colorado and Utah

signals.title: Ocean water for the desert

drivers.title: Fire gets its own agency
drivers.text: Interior launched the U.S. Wildland Fire Service in early 2026, merging its bureaus' fire programs. Budgets propose folding Forest Service fire in too, but Congress has funded the two separately and wants a feasibility study first.

dilemma.prompt: Congress asks for your view: should Forest Service wildland fire move into Interior's new fire service?

options.label: Back one fire service
options.text: Support a full merger: one command, one budget, and firefighters led by firefighters across federal lands.

options.label: Keep fire with forests
options.text: Keep fire inside the Forest Service so fuels, timber and fire planning stay integrated on the same ground.

options.label: Joint command, no merger
options.text: Create a shared USDA–Interior fire command with pooled dispatch and aviation, but keep separate agencies and budgets.

source.title: As potentially significant season kicks off, the US Wildland Fire Service's first chief shares priorities

drivers.title: Goodbye regions, hello governors
drivers.text: USDA plans to close all nine Forest Service regional offices, move headquarters to Salt Lake City and create 15 state directors to work with governors. A federal judge paused the plan in October, a ruling now under appeal.

dilemma.prompt: Your new state director asks how closely federal forest priorities should track the governor's agenda.

options.label: One shared state plan
options.text: Write a joint state–federal forest plan with the governor's office, pooling staff, budgets and priorities.

options.label: National rules first
options.text: Coordinate closely, but keep national standards and federal law as the anchor for every decision.

options.label: Delegate via Good Neighbor
options.text: Shift more project work to state crews through Good Neighbor agreements, including timber sale preparation.

source.title: Forest Service to move HQ out of DC, shutter regional offices in sweeping overhaul

drivers.title: The incredible shrinking budget
drivers.text: After losing thousands of staff in 2025, the Forest Service faces a 2027 budget request that cuts National Forest System funds about 24% and zeroes out its research and State, Private and Tribal Forestry lines.

dilemma.prompt: Money is down again. As a leadership team, what do you protect first?

options.label: Fire readiness first
options.text: Protect crews, engines and aviation; defer trail work, research and partner grants.

options.label: Keep partners whole
options.text: Protect state, Tribal and nonprofit agreements that bring outside money, even if federal crews shrink.

options.label: Fees up, sites down
options.text: Raise recreation fees and close low-use sites to keep a funded core workforce.

source.title: Chief Tom Schultz details, defends largest Forest Service reorganization in a century

drivers.title: A decade-high fire year
drivers.text: By September 5, 2026, more than 8.3 million acres had burned nationwide, the most for that date in a decade, with Oregon and Washington hit hardest. Nearly 18,000 personnel were on the lines.

dilemma.prompt: After a record fire year, do you keep a full-suppression posture or reopen room for prescribed and managed fire?

options.label: Suppress every start
options.text: Put out every fire fast to protect homes, crews and air quality; defer burning.

options.label: Reopen the burn window
options.text: Expand prescribed and managed fire with states and Tribes, accepting smoke and escape risk.

options.label: Thin, don't burn
options.text: Lean on mechanical thinning and fuel breaks near towns, with little burning.

source.title: US Wildfire Acreage Hits 10-Year High as Fires Rage Across West

drivers.title: Get the cut out
drivers.text: A 2025 executive order seeks 25% more national forest timber. Analysts find willing mills sit near only about a third of priority fire landscapes, and fire-risk gains depend on how sales are designed.

dilemma.prompt: Your timber target just rose again. How do you design this year's program?

options.label: Chase volume near mills
options.text: Concentrate sales where mills exist and logs pay, to hit the target and keep mills running.

options.label: Fuels-first sale design
options.text: Design sales around fire risk and small trees, even if volume falls short and some draw no bids.

options.label: Stewardship bundles
options.text: Bundle timber with restoration in long stewardship contracts run with local partners.

source.title: Will Increased Timber Harvesting on Federal Lands Reduce Growing Wildfire Hazards?

drivers.title: A fast lane for firesheds
drivers.text: The Fix Our Forests Act passed the House and awaits a Senate vote. If enacted, it would speed fuels and restoration work in high-risk firesheds and let larger projects skip full environmental review.

dilemma.prompt: New authority lets you skip parts of environmental review on big fireshed projects. How hard do you lean on it?

options.label: Use it to the max
options.text: Apply every new exemption to move large projects in months, not years.

options.label: Speed with consent
options.text: Use exemptions only where collaboratives, Tribes and counties already agree on the project.

options.label: Pilot and monitor
options.text: Test the authority on a few firesheds with independent monitoring before scaling up.

source.title: "Fire seasons are becoming fire years": Will Congress act?

drivers.title: The pendulum swings back
drivers.text: Federal priorities keep swinging with elections. In the 2030s, new majorities revisit recent changes: some budgets return, while reorganizations and rules reopen. Agencies face a second overhaul within a decade, and partners wonder what will stick.

dilemma.prompt: A new majority offers to restore the old structure and budgets. What do you ask for?

options.label: Restore what was lost
options.text: Rebuild regional offices, research stations and staffing toward pre-2025 levels.

options.label: Keep what works, fund it
options.text: Keep state offices and streamlined authorities, but ask for stable multi-year funding.

options.label: Lock it into law
options.text: Spend political capital writing durable statutes so the next swing cannot easily undo them.

source.title: Trying to Reason with A Midterm Election Earthquake

drivers.title: Uninsurable Main Street
drivers.text: Insurers are pulling back from fire-prone towns: Utah's 2025 nonrenewal rate led the nation and pricier surplus-lines policies keep spreading. By the 2030s, whole WUI communities struggle to find coverage or mortgages.

dilemma.prompt: Insurers will return only if communities prove lower risk. Where do you put scarce mitigation dollars?

options.label: Harden homes, certify towns
options.text: Fund home hardening and community certification so insurers can price risk down.

options.label: Treat the landscape
options.text: Put the money into fuel breaks and landscape treatments around towns.

options.label: Limit risky building
options.text: Back state limits on new construction in the highest-risk zones.

source.title: Advocates urge regulation of surplus line insurance as traditional coverage gets harder to keep

drivers.title: Wood goes vertical
drivers.text: Mass timber has grown about 20% a year since 2015, with more than 2,500 projects built or underway by the end of 2025. By the 2030s, builders want steady supplies of the small and mid-size logs restoration produces.

dilemma.prompt: A mass-timber plant will locate in your state if public forests guarantee 20 years of log supply. Do you commit?

options.label: Guarantee the supply
options.text: Sign long-term supply agreements from public forests to land the plant and its jobs.

options.label: Restoration wood only
options.text: Offer only fuels and restoration material; the plant may build smaller or go elsewhere.

options.label: Let private lands supply
options.text: Leave supply to private and family forests, with state incentives for certified wood.

source.title: 2025 Was a 'Pivotal' Year for Mass Timber Construction

drivers.title: Carbon money comes knocking
drivers.text: California extended its carbon market to 2045 and raised the offset limit, requiring at least half from in-state projects. By the 2030s, carbon buyers court every forest owner, public and private, with long contracts.

dilemma.prompt: Carbon buyers offer long-term payments to defer harvest on state and partner forests. Do you sign?

options.label: Sign the long contracts
options.text: Enroll forests in decades-long carbon contracts that pay well but lock in deferred harvest.

options.label: Credit active care only
options.text: Sell credits only from fuels reduction, reforestation and fire-resilient stands.

options.label: Keep forests flexible
options.text: Decline long contracts to keep options open for timber, fuels work and future climate shifts.

source.title: California extends cap-and-trade to 2045, renames program cap-and-invest

drivers.title: The river runs short
drivers.text: Western water keeps tightening: in 2026 Lake Powell and Lake Mead held their least combined water since 1963 after record-low snowpack, forcing Lower Basin cuts. In the 2030s, cities look upstream to forests.

dilemma.prompt: Downstream cities offer to fund thinning in their source watersheds, if those forests get top priority. Do you accept?

options.label: Follow the water money
options.text: Prioritize utility-funded watersheds; other high-risk forests wait their turn.

options.label: Pool it, treat by risk
options.text: Take the money into a shared fund and treat wherever fire risk is highest.

options.label: Manage for snow, flow
options.text: Thin stands and restore meadows to hold snow and boost late-season flows, as a monitored pilot.

source.title: Interior Department Finalizes Plans for 2027-2028 Colorado River Operations

drivers.title: Fire years, not fire seasons
drivers.text: A UN assessment projects extreme wildfires rising about 30% by 2050. By the 2040s, U.S. fire activity spans most of the year, and staffing built around summer seasonal crews no longer fits.

dilemma.prompt: Fire never really stops now. How do you staff for a year-round threat?

options.label: Year-round federal force
options.text: Convert seasonal crews into a permanent fire service that fights fire and does fuels work all year.

options.label: Community fire networks
options.text: Train and fund local, volunteer, Tribal and private crews to share response and burning.

options.label: Let remote fires work
options.text: Manage remote fires for ecological benefit and defend only communities and critical infrastructure.

source.title: UN warns that number of extreme wildfires will increase 30% by 2050, 50% by end of century
source.publisher: KTNV / Scripps News (on UNEP report "Spreading like Wildfire")

drivers.title: The next chestnut blight
drivers.text: The nursery trade keeps moving tree pathogens; sudden oak death was recently found for the first time in a Minnesota nursery. By the 2040s, an incurable pathogen establishes across a major U.S. forest type.

dilemma.prompt: A deadly pathogen is racing through a keystone tree species. What is your strategy?

options.label: Contain at all costs
options.text: Quarantine, cut buffer zones and restrict nursery and firewood movement across state lines.

options.label: Breed resistant trees
options.text: Invest in resistant and gene-edited trees with Tribes and universities, accepting public debate.

options.label: Salvage and diversify
options.text: Salvage dying stands fast and replant mixed species suited to the future climate.

source.title: Biosurveillance project flags first sudden oak death detection in Minnesota
source.publisher: Minnesota Invasive Terrestrial Plants and Pests Center, University of Minnesota

drivers.title: Algorithms on the fireline
drivers.text: The first operational FireSat satellites launched in 2026, aiming for hourly global coverage by 2029. By the 2040s, AI spots nearly every ignition within minutes and recommends where to thin, burn and dispatch.

dilemma.prompt: AI can now triage initial attack and rank treatments faster than any team. How much decision power do you give it?

options.label: Let the model dispatch
options.text: Automate initial attack and treatment ranking; people audit the decisions afterward.

options.label: Humans make the call
options.text: Use AI as an advisor; trained people make and explain every decision.

options.label: Open the data commons
options.text: Share models and data openly with Tribes, states, landowners and insurers.

source.title: Muon Space Deploys First Three Operational FireSat Satellites for Earth Fire Alliance

drivers.title: Co-management goes mainstream
drivers.text: Co-stewardship keeps spreading across administrations, like the Cow Creek Umpqua Tribe's 155,000-acre agreement on two Oregon national forests. By the 2040s, Tribes co-manage large areas of national forest, with cultural fire built in.

dilemma.prompt: Tribal nations propose taking the lead in managing several national forest units. How do you respond?

options.label: Transfer lead authority
options.text: Support Tribes as lead managers, with federal funding and treaty-based standards.

options.label: Joint boards, shared budgets
options.text: Create co-management boards where federal and Tribal leaders decide together.

options.label: Grow agreements gradually
options.text: Keep the federal lead but widen co-stewardship agreements unit by unit.

source.title: Cow Creek Umpqua signs 155,000-acre forest co-stewardship agreement with U.S. Forest Service

drivers.title: Hand the keys to the states
drivers.text: Proposals to sell or transfer federal lands keep resurfacing; a 2025 Senate plan was dropped after bipartisan pushback. By the 2040s, Congress lets willing states take over management of some national forests.

dilemma.prompt: Congress offers your state management of the national forests within its borders. Do you take it?

options.label: Accept, with federal funding
options.text: Take over management only with guaranteed federal funding and current public access.

options.label: Decline, stay a partner
options.text: Stay a partner, not the owner; keep national rules and federal funding.

options.label: Accept, allow some sales
options.text: Take over and allow limited land sales for housing and state revenue.

source.title: Sen. Mike Lee removes public lands provision from Trump's "big, beautiful bill"

scenarios.name: Today's Trajectory
scenarios.summary: Starts from conditions in late 2026: a decade-high fire year, a Forest Service about one-sixth smaller after 2025 departures, a court-paused reorganization, a new Interior fire service, stopgap budgets, rising timber targets, Colorado River shortages and a newly elected Congress. Drivers extend current trends without assuming which political direction wins.

scenarios.name: Lean Federal Era
scenarios.summary: Washington keeps shrinking its footprint: leaner budgets, consolidated fire, fewer staff and faster approvals. Supporters see efficiency, more timber and local control; critics see lost capacity, science and public services. Markets, states and private owners fill gaps unevenly. Can partners do more with less federal help?

scenarios.name: States & Tribes Lead
scenarios.summary: Authority shifts toward governors and Tribal nations. State offices replace regions, Good Neighbor and co-stewardship agreements carry most project work, and Tribes lead cultural fire on more ground. Federal funding is uncertain and rules differ state to state. Partnerships are strong; consistency and national standards are tested.

scenarios.name: Restoration Economy
scenarios.summary: Money and demand line up behind active restoration: streamlined fireshed projects, a mass-timber building boom, carbon payments and steadier multi-year funding. Mills reopen and crews grow. The risks are overpromised log supply, carbon-contract lock-in and boom-bust cycles if markets or politics turn.

scenarios.name: Climate Whiplash
scenarios.summary: Nature sets the agenda. With a record-strength El Niño, 2026 runs above 1.5°C of warming, and drought, deluge and fire alternate faster than plans adapt. Water shortages, pests and insurance retreat stack up. Institutions are intact but stretched. Can leaders adapt fast enough to keep the system from unraveling?

roles.title: Forest Supervisor
roles.org: USDA Forest Service — a national forest
roles.bio: Line officer for a national forest of a million-plus acres, balancing timber, fire, water, recreation, grazing, and Tribal consultation under federal law, with a thinner staff and more acres burning each decade.

mandates.why: Restoration at scale: heal the landscape, keep the work paying for itself, and protect downstream water, without closing the forest to the public.
Multiple use and public trust: a forest people visit, Congress funds, and downstream users rely on.

ability.name: Line Officer's Decision
ability.text: Once per game: you sign the decision memo. Decide one Dilemma outright, overriding the vote.

future.holding: Forest Supervisor, Still Answering Every Phone

roles.title: Federal Wildland Fire Director
roles.org: Federal wildland fire program (Forest Service or a consolidated federal fire service)
roles.bio: Leads federal wildland fire for a region: suppression, fuels, prescribed fire, aviation, and crews. Whether the program stays in the Forest Service or moves to a unified federal fire agency, the job is safe, effective fire on the land.

mandates.why: Fire-adapted landscapes: fewer destructive fires, a seasoned workforce, and communities ready for the smoke and flames that will still come.
A durable fire organization: stable funding and a career workforce, whatever the org chart says, without losing public trust.

ability.name: Stop the Spread
ability.text: Once per game: initial attack holds. Cancel one negative effect from a System Response cascade as it happens.

roles.title: Forest Service Research Station Director
roles.bio: Directs a research station's scientists, experimental forests, and inventory data. Turns science into tools managers actually use, while protecting decades-long monitoring records through budget swings and reorganizations.

mandates.why: Adaptation science: understand what climate is doing to forests and keep the people and data to act on it.
Science to practice: research embedded with managers, Tribes, and universities, and funded long enough to matter.

ability.name: Horizon Scan
ability.text: Once per game: discard your hand and draw three Signals from the Far horizon.

roles.title: State Forester
roles.bio: Runs the state forestry agency: fire on state and private land, service forestry for family landowners, urban forests, and trust lands. Partners with the Forest Service through Shared Stewardship and answers to a governor and legislature.

mandates.why: Shared stewardship: one plan across ownerships, fewer catastrophic fires, and a forest economy that pays for the work.
Keep forests as forests: healthy woods, safe communities, and steady state authority and funding for both.

ability.name: Forest Action Plan
ability.text: Once per game: bring new options to the table. Replace up to two strategies in the Council market.

roles.title: State Fire & Good Neighbor Program Manager
roles.org: State forestry agency — fire and cross-boundary programs
roles.bio: Manages Good Neighbor agreements and cross-boundary fire programs, putting state crews, contractors, and sale staff to work on federal land and reinvesting receipts in the next restoration project.

mandates.why: Cross-boundary work: crews and agreements that treat whole firesheds, not just one ownership at a time.
A Good Neighbor economy: timber receipts and local contractors fund more restoration, without trading away carbon.

ability.name: Good Neighbor Agreement
ability.text: Once per game: shared crews and receipts cut the cost of one Partnership-tagged strategy by 2.

roles.title: Tribal Natural Resources Director
roles.org: Natural resources department of a sovereign Tribal Nation
roles.bio: Leads natural resources for a sovereign Tribal Nation: forestry, fisheries, cultural fire, first foods, and treaty-reserved rights. Negotiates co-stewardship with federal and state agencies government-to-government, grounded in Indigenous knowledge.

mandates.why: Cultural fire and co-stewardship: Tribal authority on the ground and good fire returned to the land.
Homelands and first foods: healthy forests, clean water, and a stable climate for the generations to come.

ability.name: Cultural Fire Knowledge
ability.text: Once per game: practitioners bring generations of knowledge. +2 to Fire & Fuels, Forest Health, or Partnerships.

roles.title: County Commissioner
roles.org: Board of Commissioners of a forest-dependent county
roles.bio: Elected commissioner of a rural county that is mostly federal land. Balances road, school, and emergency budgets tied to timber receipts and federal payments, and lives with the results of every fire season and mill decision.

mandates.why: A working rural economy: mill jobs, visitors, and a tax base that keeps schools and roads open.
A safe, fire-adapted county: hardened homes, evacuation routes, and reliable federal and state partners to pay for them.

ability.name: Field Hearing
ability.text: Once per game: the county brings the delegation to town. Cancel one negative effect of an Era Driver as it happens.

roles.title: Water Utility General Manager
roles.bio: Runs a water utility serving several hundred thousand people whose drinking water begins on national forest land. Treats post-fire sediment and shrinking snowpack as ratepayer costs, and invests upstream through watershed partnerships.

mandates.why: Source-water security: fewer fires in the watershed and reservoirs that do not fill with ash.
Watershed investment: ratepayer dollars and partners restoring the upper basin as snowpack shifts.

ability.name: Source Water Protection
ability.text: Once per game: the utility stands guard. Protect Water, Forest Health, or Fire & Fuels from Signal effects until the era ends.

roles.title: Mill & Mass Timber Executive
roles.org: Family-owned sawmill and mass timber manufacturer
roles.bio: Operates a family sawmill and a new cross-laminated timber plant. Needs predictable log supply, including small-diameter restoration wood, skilled workers, and building codes and buyers that favor wood.

mandates.why: Mass timber growth: restoration wood becomes buildings that store carbon and keep a mill town working.
Supply certainty: steady federal and state volume, a trained workforce, and a mill that survives the next fire.

ability.name: Order Book
ability.text: Once per game: a signed purchase order de-risks the deal. Reduce the cost of one Wood-tagged strategy by 2.

roles.title: Family Forest Owners Association President
roles.bio: Volunteer president of an association of family woodland owners — retirees, ranchers, heirs — who together own much of the state's forest. Champions technical help, fair markets, fire safety, and keeping land in the family.

mandates.why: Markets for working woodlands: timber and carbon income that make it worth keeping the land as forest.
Fire-safe family forests: woodlots the family still enjoys, and neighbors protected when fire comes over the ridge.

ability.name: Ground Truth
ability.text: Once per game: landowners on the ground say 'not here.' Cancel one negative effect of a Signal as it is played.

roles.title: Conservation Alliance Director
roles.bio: Leads a coalition of conservation groups focused on old forests, wildlife, and climate refugia. Has sued agencies and signed collaborative agreements with them, sometimes the same year, and brings philanthropy and scientists to the table.

mandates.why: Climate refugia: intact, connected forests that store carbon and shelter species, built through collaboration rather than litigation.
Collaboration over conflict: a broad public that loves these forests and partners who restore them together.

ability.name: Philanthropic Match
ability.text: Once per game: a foundation matches the table. Gain 2 extra Capacity in this era's Council.

roles.title: Outdoor Recreation Coalition Director
roles.org: Coalition of outfitters, user groups, and gateway businesses
roles.bio: Speaks for outfitters, trail groups, gateway-town businesses, and millions of visitors. Pushes for maintained trails, fair access, and fees that stay local, and needs open, safe, smoke-free forests to keep the recreation economy running.

mandates.why: Access for all: open trails and staffed sites that welcome everyone and keep gateway towns thriving.
A recreation economy that funds stewardship: rivers, trails, and fee dollars working together.

ability.name: Rally the Public
ability.text: Once per game: public attention shifts. Move up to 2 points from one domain to another.

strategies.title: All-lands fuels treatment
strategies.text: Thin and burn hazardous fuels across federal, state, Tribal, and private land in the firesheds that threaten the most homes and water supplies.

strategies.title: Shared Stewardship compact
strategies.text: State and Forest Service leaders sign joint priorities, share data and staff, and plan treatments together across the whole landscape.

strategies.title: Tribal co-stewardship agreements
strategies.text: Government-to-government agreements give Tribal Nations lasting stewardship roles, co-management where law allows, and fund cultural burning and Indigenous knowledge in planning and monitoring.

strategies.title: Community wildfire defense
strategies.text: Fund community wildfire protection plans, home hardening, defensible space, and evacuation routes in the highest-risk neighborhoods.

strategies.title: Conservation corps pipeline
strategies.text: Paid youth, veteran, and Tribal crews with apprenticeships that lead to permanent agency, contractor, and fire jobs.

strategies.title: Listen-first public engagement
strategies.text: Listening sessions, open project dashboards, and youth programs rebuild trust before the next controversial project or fire season.

strategies.title: Good Neighbor expansion
strategies.text: States, counties, and Tribes do restoration and timber work on national forests, reinvesting receipts into the next project.

strategies.title: Workforce housing partnership
strategies.text: Agencies, counties, and nonprofits build housing so seasonal and permanent staff can afford to live near the forests they manage.

strategies.title: Local restoration contractors
strategies.text: Multi-year stewardship contracts give local logging and restoration businesses the certainty to hire, buy equipment, and stay.

strategies.title: River & trail stewardship partners
strategies.text: Outfitters, user groups, and volunteers adopt trails and river reaches, fixing erosion and reporting problems in exchange for access.

strategies.title: Outdoor access & equity
strategies.text: Shuttles, accessible trails, multilingual programs, and school partnerships bring new and underserved visitors to public lands.

strategies.title: Beaver & meadow restoration
strategies.text: Low-tech, process-based restoration (beaver dam analogs, wet meadows, riparian buffers) stores water, cools streams, and slows fire.

strategies.title: Burn-boss pipeline & liability reform
strategies.text: Training exchanges, state liability standards, and a burn claims fund put more good fire on the ground, at the cost of more smoke days.

strategies.title: Utility watershed investment fund
strategies.text: Water utilities add a ratepayer charge to co-fund thinning, burning, and restoration in the source watersheds they depend on.

strategies.title: Small-wood & biomass markets
strategies.text: Incentives for biochar, pellets, and combined heat and power make thinning small trees pay, though burning biomass adds emissions.

strategies.title: Litigation-resilient planning
strategies.text: Invest in strong analysis, early collaboration, and objection resolution so landscape projects hold up in court, at a real cost in staff time.

strategies.title: Recreation fee reinvestment
strategies.text: Modernize trails and campgrounds, keep fee revenue local, and market gateway towns, bringing more visitors and more wear on fragile sites.

strategies.title: Family forest carbon program
strategies.text: Enroll small landowners in high-integrity carbon programs that pay for deferred harvest and better management, trimming near-term log supply.

strategies.title: Year-round fire workforce
strategies.text: Permanent pay, year-round crews, housing, and mental-health support keep experienced firefighters, but compete for scarce budget dollars.

strategies.title: Accelerated timber output
strategies.text: Raise harvest targets and streamline approvals to boost volume quickly, strengthening mills and county receipts but straining habitat and trail access.

strategies.title: Mature & old-growth safeguards
strategies.text: Durable protection for old and mature stands and roadless areas, paired with active stewardship around them, reducing some timber supply.

strategies.title: Pest early detection & rapid response
strategies.text: Trap networks, detector dogs, and fast strike teams catch invasive insects and diseases early; quarantines restrict log and firewood movement.

strategies.title: Post-fire recovery strike teams
strategies.text: Interagency teams stabilize burned slopes, warn downstream towns of debris flows, and replant with utility and Tribal partners.

strategies.title: Lean operations consolidation
strategies.text: Close or merge offices and shift functions to regional hubs, saving money fast but thinning local staff and visitor services.

strategies.title: Nursery & reforestation surge
strategies.text: Expand seed collection, nurseries, and planting crews to close the post-fire reforestation backlog with climate-informed stock.

strategies.title: AI & remote-sensing early warning
strategies.text: Satellites, cameras, and drones with machine-learning detection flag new ignitions, beetle kill, and drought stress early, and share the data openly.

strategies.title: Seed banks & assisted migration
strategies.text: Bank genetically diverse seed, test climate-adapted sources in trial plantings, and update seed-zone rules for a warmer future.

strategies.title: Science-to-practice partnerships
strategies.text: Research stations, universities, and extension embed scientists with managers to co-design treatments and monitor what works.

strategies.title: Working-forest conservation finance
strategies.text: Blend Forest Legacy, state, philanthropic, and private capital into easements that keep family and industrial forests working and intact.

strategies.title: Climate-ready forest plans
strategies.text: Revise land management plans around climate scenarios, drought refugia, and carbon, accepting slower project approvals while plans change.

strategies.title: Mass timber procurement standard
strategies.text: Public buildings specify mass timber made from restoration wood, giving mills a steady buyer and storing carbon in schools and housing.

strategies.title: Stable fire & land budgets
strategies.text: A broad coalition wins predictable multi-year funding so suppression costs stop draining fuels, research, and recreation programs.

strategies.title: WUI land-use & insurance compact
strategies.text: State codes, county zoning, and insurer discounts reward fire-adapted development: a hard political lift with lasting payoff.

strategies.title: Unified federal fire service
strategies.text: Consolidate federal wildland fire into one agency with common standards and careers: promising efficiency, risking disruption to shared crews and land-management ties.

strategies.title: Forest resilience bond
strategies.text: Private investors front the cost of restoration; utilities, agencies, and insurers repay them as avoided-fire benefits arrive.

cascades.text: A growing fire deficit: big fires keep burning through source watersheds and into towns.
Heat and drought outrun adaptation: drought stress and beetles keep killing trees.
Dead and dying stands become fuel and turn from carbon sink to source.
Ash-choked reservoirs and drying streams hit towns and riparian forests.
The last mill closes; loggers and the restoration workforce leave with it.
Rural distress and insurance retreat erode the tax base and the public's patience.
No one left to staff crews or keep agreements alive.
Trust collapses into lawsuits and go-it-alone projects.
A united coalition makes the budget case together and wins.
A timber boom pays wages and county bills, and pulls harvest toward older stands.
Record crowds create new champions for the forest, and new wear on fragile places.
Thriving towns sprawl deeper into fire country: more homes and ignitions to defend.
